Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson is doubling down on buying the selloff after the S&P 500 broke below his 7,100 downside target. In Monday's note, his team called it "the fat pitch we have patiently been waiting for, and we're not going to miss it," adding that "markets bottom on bad news and deleveraging. We have had a lot of both" (via Bloomberg).

How we got here:

▪️ In late September, he warned of a drop to as low as 7,100 before the bull market resumed.
▪️ In early November, he said the correction was in its final innings, with a 7,100 to 7,300 range. On November 16, he raised his 12-month target to 8,700.
▪️ On Friday, the S&P 500 closed at 6,910.39, 2.7% below the bottom of that range and 11.6% below the October 6 record. That capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest since February 2020.

Why he's pressing the call rather than backing off:

▪️ He calls the break below his range an overshoot of fair value, driven by forced deleveraging. His team is more bullish tactically than at any time since early April.
▪️ Sentiment: his sentiment indicator hit −1.6 and the VIX hit 36, both matching December 2018, and hedge fund positioning is similarly washed out.
▪️ Valuation: the S&P 500's forward P/E has dropped from nearly 23 in late October to 16.5, below its 17.4 long-run average. The Nasdaq 100 is under 17, below its pandemic low.
▪️ Earnings: by his math, stocks are pricing in about a 6% drop in 2027 earnings. He forecasts 14% growth, and consensus is 17%.
▪️ He likes hyperscalers, industrials, quality cyclicals with improving estimates, and companies benefiting from AI adoption.
▪️ The main risk is still a hawkish Fed. But he thinks market pricing is "far too hawkish" and expects a calmer message in December than some fear.

The history backs him, with a catch. Since 1990, the VIX has had 17 episodes where it first closed at 35 or higher (Friday's close was 35.89):

▪️ The S&P 500 was higher 12 months later in 14 of the 17, with a median gain of 21.6%. That compares with 11.9% for any 12-month stretch since 1990.
▪️ December 2018, the episode he compares this one to, was followed by a 37.1% gain.
▪️ But the first spike often wasn't the low. In 8 of the 17, the S&P 500 fell more than 5% further within three months, including another 34.9% in 2008 and 24.9% in 2020.
▪️ The three losing years were 2001 and 2008, both earnings recessions, and 2022, a Fed hiking cycle.

History would indicate his call should hold unless earnings roll over or the Fed gets much more aggressive. The market is already pricing in an earnings drop he doesn't expect, so the bigger swing factor is the Fed, the one risk he concedes. 

Morgan Stanley chief economist Seth Carpenter acknowledged in his Sunday Start note (via ZeroHedge) that clients pushed back hard on the bank's "Embracing Risk" outlook, and that even if the bank is right, the path through 2027 "will not be smooth or linear."

▪️ Liquidity, the one he ranks most important, hasn’t cleared. ▪️ Wilson notes median Russell 3000 earnings growth is running 14%, the strongest in four years.

CBOE's Mandy Xu: Friday’s VIX move, while large, was  surprisingly orderly. The sell-off in SPX® spot (-3.7%) and the  increase in fixed-strike vols (+3.2 pts) accounted for almost  90% of the 7.4pt VIX increase. 

Very little came from demand for downside puts. In fact, changes in skew and convexity contributed just 0.9pt to the VIX move (see Exhibit 2). In contrast, demand for downside protection made up almost half of the Nov 5th VIX spike. This can also be seen in  measures of SPX 1M skew (25-delta ratio), which spiked to  the 95th percentile high after the Nov 5th sell-off but only  steepened modestly to the 80th percentile last Friday. 

Also  notable was the lack of demand for upside calls on Friday, with call skew falling and call convexity unchanged. It seems that while there was little panic on Friday, investors were also not positioning for a quick rebound.

Another factor arguing for a bounce this week is the seasonality breakdown from @AlmanacTrader, editor of the Stock Trader’s Almanac & Almanac Investor Newsletter, Thanksgiving week has historically been one of November’s strongest.

Monday is trading day 16. Over the past 21 years, the major indices have averaged gains on every trading day of the holiday-shortened week. That adds up to about 1.35–1.4% for the DJIA, S&P 500, Nasdaq and Russell 1000, and about 1.8% for the Russell 2000. Tuesday has been the best day, adding about 0.5–0.65%. Wednesday and the half-session Friday after Thanksgiving have each added about 0.2–0.4%.

Midterm years though have been less strong though. The Nasdaq has gained about 1.25% and the Russell 2000 about 1.1%, while the Russell 1000 has added about 0.85% and the DJIA and S&P only 0.4–0.55%. The DJIA, S&P and Russell 1000 have dipped slightly on Wednesday, but every midterm line has risen on Friday. 

Hirsch notes that recent weakness around Thanksgiving has shifted DJIA and S&P strength to look more like the Nasdaq and Russell 2000. His advice is to go long into any weakness before the holiday and exit into strength just before or after.

The month then wraps up Monday, Nov. 30 (day 20), which has added another 0.2–0.4% across all years. One caution: this year day 20 is also the Monday after Thanksgiving, and that Monday has been higher in just 5 of the past 21 years (an average −0.6%), and 29 of 76 since 1950, by our calculations.

This year, though, the seasonal script has gone badly off course. Through Friday, the S&P 500 is down 8.8% for November, compared with about +0.45% for its 21-year average and +1.75% for midterm years at the same point. 

If November ended at Friday's level, it would be the S&P 500’s worst November since 1973 (−11.4%), worse than 1987 (−8.5%), 2000 (−8.0%) and 2008 (−7.5%). Even a full seasonal rally from here, about 1.7% across all years, would leave the index down roughly 7% for the month.

Ahead of Friday's expiration, Tier1Alpha counted 37 other times since 2012 that the S&P 500 was in negative gamma heading into monthly expiration with the VIX above 20. In 81% of them, the VIX was lower a week later and stayed below its pre-expiration level over the following month, and in 68% it closed back below 20 at least once along the way.

My own numbers point the same way, with a caveat on timing. Without Tier1Alpha's gamma filter, the VIX was lower a week later after 72% of the 47 monthly expirations since 2012 with the VIX above 20, and lower a month later after 72%, while it closed back below 20 within a month 62% of the time.

From 30 or higher, as on Friday, it has taken much longer to get back below 20. In the six such cases since 2012, the VIX was lower a week later every time and a month later in five, but only one (December 2018) got back below 20 within a month. 

Going back to 1990, the VIX was lower 20 sessions after a 30+ expiration 80% of the time (24 of 30), by a median 5.6 points, but December 2018 is still the only one that closed below 20 within a month. Counting only the first expiration in each run, it took a median of 107 sessions, or about five months, to close below 20.

@C_Barraud's Morning Brief is packed with posts about the equity selloff (along with a lot of other stuff) including @MikeZaccardi's post that Goldman's US Financial Conditions Index excluding equities hit a new cycle high, "along with intensely bearish Fed speak."

That fits with the analysis I ran in the Week Ahead:
▪ Goldman's headline FCI tightened 46bp last week to 99.53, the biggest weekly tightening since March 2020 and the ninth-largest since 1990, leaving it the tightest since April 2025.
▪ Stocks did most of it (about 35bp from Monday's close through Friday), with, with credit spreads and the dollar adding about 5bp each and lower long-term yields offsetting about 9bp.
▪ The ex-equities line shows conditions outside of stocks were already tight. Goldman says the two series "diverged" over the past few years, but "both series have tightened in recent months."
▪ The Fed's own FCI-G said the same thing in October: stocks supplied 96% of what was left of the tailwind to growth, everything else netted to about zero, and interest rates had turned into a drag.
▪ But the Fed isn't backing off. By my count all 16 of the 19 FOMC participants who have spoken on rates since the November 5 selloff have signaled more tightening, and Philadelphia's Paulson, one of the most dovish members, said Friday she'd be open to considering back-to-back hikes.

So we've clearly not gotten to the point of a "Fed put," but with the biggest accommodative factor quickly losing steam, the words "policy mistake" are being uttered more and more. 

One silver lining: after the 12 prior weeks since 1990 when Goldman's FCI tightened 41bp or more, the S&P 500 was higher three months later 11 times (median +6.5%, about double normal), though the first week was a coin flip and October 2008 was the big exception.

South Korea's exports topped $1T for the first time, making it only the fourth country to reach the mark, after the US, China and Germany per Bloomberg.

What stands out is how small Korea's economy is next to the rest of the club:

▪️ The IMF puts Korea's 2026 GDP at ~$2.25T, about 7% the size of the US economy, about a tenth of China's and about 40% of Germany's.
▪️ At the current pace Korea finishes 2026 near $1.15T (+~62% y/y). That's ~51% of GDP, vs ~34% for Germany, ~19% for China and ~7% for the US.
▪️ That works out to ~$22K of exports per person, edging past Germany (~$21K) and far above the US (~$6K) and China (~$3K).
▪️ In 2025 Korea was the world's 8th-largest exporter at $710B, behind the Netherlands, Hong Kong, Japan and Italy. This year it passes all four.

As you might guess, semiconductors are the main engine:

▪️ Chip exports hit $56.4B in October, up 259% y/y and 49% of all exports. For 2025 as a whole the share was 24%, itself a record.
▪️ Chip exports for January–October (~$397B) are already more than double the total for all of 2025 ($173B).
▪️ Much of it is price rather than volume. Bank of Korea data show electronics export values rising far faster than volumes as memory chip prices climb.
▪️ October's 93.7% jump in total exports was the biggest since 1974. By my math, chips supplied ~73% of the $56B y/y gain, AI-server-heavy computer exports (+497%) ~9%, and petroleum products (+80% to $6.9B) ~6%.
▪️ Non-chip exports rose 34% in October, though two extra working days helped. The petroleum surge is mostly oil prices (EIA has Brent averaging $97 this year vs $69 in 2025), and much of it washes out because Korea imports the crude: its energy imports jumped 86% in early November.

Korea's leverage to the AI trade is what makes its trade data, published at the 10- and 20-day marks each month, a key early read on that cycle (Chair Warsh noted he was watching Korea's economy at the October FOMC press conference, as it tells him "what is on planes and ships coming this way"). Two things to watch:

▪️ Momentum. Daily exports adjusted for working days eased to $5.24B in October from September's record $5.63B. The first 10 days of November ($33.5B, a record for that stretch) show no stall yet. Monday's November 1–20 figures are the next check.
▪️ Concentration. The boom hasn't reached Korean households. Q3 GDP beat at +1% q/q, but private consumption shrank. That's the backdrop for Thursday's Bank of Korea decision.
